subject: Arabic
source: Drive: Curriculum/Arabic folder and Secondary Lesson Plan - Arabic - Y8 (format and approach); National Curriculum early language learning

lessons.title: Greetings: As-salaamu alaykum
objectives: Say and respond to the Islamic greeting
Say hello, good morning and goodbye in Arabic
Use a kind face and a smile when greeting

keywords.def: and peace be upon you too

starter: Let us all say Bismillah together. Can you say it?
Wave hello to a friend on screen. How do we feel when someone smiles at us?
Which language do we say Bismillah in? (Arabic)

teach.heading: Arabic is a special language
bullets: Arabic is the language of the Qur'an
We can say hello in Arabic
teach.note: Start with Bismillah. Show a big, friendly Arabic word on screen. Say: today we learn a new language that Muslims all over the world use. Keep it playful. Pupils echo each word after you.

teach.heading: As-salaamu alaykum
bullets: It means: peace be upon you
teach.note: Model slowly, say it three times, pupils echo. Point to the screen as you say each word. Ask: what do we want for our friends? (peace, kindness). Do not worry about letter reading; this is listening and speaking.

teach.heading: The answer
bullets: It means: and peace on you too
teach.note: Explain we always answer. Teacher says the greeting, class answers; then swap. Qur'an 4:86 teaches us to reply with a greeting as good or better, say this simply as 'Allah tells us to answer kindly'.

teach.heading: More greetings
teach.note: Use actions: wave for marhaban, stretch and yawn for good morning, wave goodbye. Pupils copy actions and words. Misconception: pupils may mix the words, so repeat in a quick-fire game.

teach.heading: Spreading salaam
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ told us to spread salaam
Spreading salaam helps us love each other
teach.note: Hadith: the Prophet ﷺ said to spread salaam among yourselves so that you love one another (Sahih Muslim). Tell this in simple words. Ask: who can we say salaam to at home today?

practice: Teacher says 'as-salaamu alaykum' to each child in turn; child answers 'wa alaykumu s-salaam'.
Match the word to the action: wave, yawn, wave goodbye - say the Arabic.
independent: Pupils greet a partner in the breakout room with salaam and a smile.
Show a teddy or toy to the camera and greet it in Arabic.
Draw a picture of two friends saying salaam and hold it up to the camera.
exit: What do we say when someone says 'as-salaamu alaykum'?
What do we say in the morning: marhaban or sabaahul khayr?
lessons.homework: Say as-salaamu alaykum to three family members and tell us how they answered.
lessons.send: SEND: use picture cards and actions, accept pointing or whispering. EAL: say the word and the English together. Stretch: ask pupils to greet in the morning and in the evening.

lessons.title: My name and how are you?

keywords.def: what is your name? (to a boy)
what is your name? (to a girl)

starter: How do we greet our teacher in Arabic?
What do we answer to 'as-salaamu alaykum'?
How do we say 'good morning' in Arabic?

teach.heading: Saying our name
teach.note: Model with your own name. Pupils put their name after 'ismee'. Use puppets. Name sounds like 'Ahmad' and 'Maryam' are easy to say. Misconception: pupils say 'my ismee' - remind that ismee already means 'my name'.

teach.heading: What is your name?
teach.note: Introduce that Arabic has a different ending for boy and girl: -ka for a boy and -ki for a girl. Do not explain grammar; just model by pointing at a boy then a girl. Practise in a circle with a ball.

teach.heading: How are you?
bullets: Answer: أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ - ana bi-khayr (I am well)
teach.note: Use faces: happy face for bi-khayr. Say it with a smile. Ask pupils how they feel today and encourage them to answer ana bi-khayr.

teach.heading: Alhamdu lillah
bullets: We thank Allah for our blessings
teach.note: Explain that we say this when we are well and happy; it reminds us to thank Allah. Link to everyday life: when we finish eating, when we feel well. Keep to age-level language.

teach.heading: Thank you
teach.note: Role-play passing an object: giver says 'tafaddal' optionally; receiver says shukran; giver says afwan. Praise good manners (adab).

practice: Class chant: ismee ... (each child says their name).
Teacher asks 'kayfa haaluka?' to three children; they answer 'ana bi-khayr, alhamdu lillah'.
independent: Pass a soft toy: ask 'maa ismuka?' then answer 'ismee ...' and pass on.
Make a happy face and a sad face. Say the Arabic for 'I am well' when you show the happy face.
Say shukran and afwan to a partner when you give them a pencil.
exit: How do you say 'my name is Yusuf' in Arabic? (ismee Yusuf)
What do we say after someone asks 'kayfa haaluka?'
lessons.homework: Ask a family member 'kayfa haaluka?' and tell us what they said.
lessons.send: SEND: use name cards and picture prompts; allow pupils to nod or point. EAL: pair with a confident speaker. Stretch: use both 'ismee' and 'ana bi-khayr' in one sentence.

lessons.title: Letters: Alif, Baa and Taa
objectives: Recognise and say the sounds of أ ب ت
Say a word that starts with each letter
Trace each letter in the air

keywords.def: the second letter, sound 'b', one dot below
the third letter, sound 't', two dots above

starter: How do we say hello in Arabic?
How do we say 'my name is' in Arabic?
What do we say to thank someone?

teach.heading: Arabic letters
bullets: We read from right to left
teach.note: Show a page of Arabic and point to the right-hand side, trace with your finger from right to left. Have pupils trace right to left in the air. Ask: which hand starts? (right)

teach.heading: Alif أ
teach.note: Model sound 'a' with fatha (a short line above). Hop like a rabbit saying arnab. Draw the alif as a tall stick. Misconception: alif is not the same as English 'A' shape; it looks like a straight line.

teach.heading: Baa ب
teach.note: Quack like a duck and say batta. Show the letter shaped like a boat with one dot underneath. Point to the dot and say 'one dot below'. Pupils copy on whiteboards or in the air.

teach.heading: Taa ت
teach.note: Pretend to bite an apple. Show two dots above. Compare with baa: same boat shape, different dots. Quick game: teacher holds up fingers 1 below / 2 above, pupils say b or t.

teach.heading: Sound game
teach.note: Show the three words with pictures. Pupils say the first sound. Then play 'which letter?': teacher says a word, pupils point to the correct letter on their card.

practice: Hold up alif, baa, taa cards; class says each sound.
Teacher says arnab, batta, tuffaaha; pupils show the matching picture card.
independent: Trace each letter in the air three times, saying its sound.
Draw an apple and write a taa next to it with two dots.
Find something at home that starts with 'b' (e.g. باب - baab, door) and show it.
exit: Which letter has one dot below?
Which letter is the first sound of tuffaaha?
lessons.homework: Draw a rabbit, a duck and an apple. Write the correct Arabic letter beside each one.
lessons.send: SEND: large letter cards, colour the dots, use tracing in sand/air. EAL: say the English word then the Arabic word. Stretch: think of one more word that starts with each sound.

lessons.title: Counting 1 to 5 in Arabic
objectives: Say the numbers one to five in Arabic
Link counting to the five daily prayers
starter: Which letter has two dots above: baa or taa?
What is a rabbit called in Arabic?
How do we say 'thank you' in Arabic?

teach.heading: Let us count
teach.note: Show one finger, two fingers, three fingers. Teach each number with a clap. Pupils echo. Say the numbers slowly then faster. Keep numerals on screen: 1, 2, 3 (note that Arabic numerals also appear as ١ ٢ ٣ but do not require reading them today).

teach.heading: Four and five
teach.note: Use fingers and objects. Explain khamsa with five fingers on one hand. Common error: pupils say 'khamsa' with an 'h' like 'ham'; model the throaty 'kh'.

teach.heading: Counting song
teach.note: Chant 1 to 5 together with a clap. Repeat in reverse (5 to 1). Challenge: whisper the odd numbers, say the even ones out loud.

teach.heading: Five daily prayers
bullets: We pray خَمْس صَلَوَات - khams salawaat
teach.note: Link counting to the five daily prayers. Ask pupils to count the prayers on fingers in Arabic. Keep it gentle and positive. Do not test pupils on their own practice.

teach.heading: Count the things
teach.note: Show pictures of apples and ducks. Pupils count in Arabic. If needed, allow them to say just the number. Do not worry about the grammar of counted nouns in Reception.

practice: Hold up letter cards alif, baa, taa and say the sounds.
independent: Count the objects the teacher shows on the screen in Arabic.
Show the correct number of fingers when the teacher says the number.
Clap the number of times you hear: ithnaan, khamsa, waahid.
exit: How many fingers do we show for 'arba'a'?
lessons.homework: Count the toys or fruit at home in Arabic and tell the class how many there were.
lessons.send: SEND: use finger counting and objects; accept clapping. EAL: say the English numbers alongside. Stretch: count backwards from five to one.
